query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the HVOF spray parameters—specifically by reducing the stand‐off distance and increasing the in‐flight particle temperature and velocity—will produce a thicker FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat compared to the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock, while preserving coating integrity and limiting as‐sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy feedstock (15–45 μm) deposited by HVOF with currently suboptimal thickness and oxidation limited by typical processing parameters.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVOF spraying parameters by reducing the stand‐off distance and increasing both the particle temperature and velocity to enhance particle melting and kinetic energy on impact.
generation.conditions: This intervention should be effective under standard thermal-spray deposition conditions for bond coats in thermal barrier systems, where the oxygen partial pressure is controlled and the substrate is maintained at temperatures typical of service in high-temperature aerospace or turbine environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced melting and higher kinetic energy of the particles will promote better splat flattening and inter-splat bonding, resulting in a thicker, denser coating, while the reduced in-flight residence time in an oxidizing environment minimizes excess oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The increased particle temperature and velocity lead to improved deposition efficiency and splat deformation that builds up coating thickness. Simultaneously, a reduced stand-off distance shortens the high-temperature flight time, thereby limiting exposure to oxygen and minimizing unwanted oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HVOF process is predicted to yield a deposited bond coat with a thickness significantly exceeding the baseline 15–45 μm range, while maintaining microstructural integrity and low levels of as-sprayed oxidation relative to conventional parameters.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced from 15–45 μm feedstock using standard HVOF parameters, which currently result in insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only within the operational window of HVOF spraying where the adjustments maintain acceptable thermal gradients and oxygen exposure. Extreme parameter changes (e.g., excessively high particle temperatures or very short stand-off distances) might compromise coating adhesion or lead to excessive oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal window for stand-off distance, particle temperature, and velocity to maximize thickness without incurring additional oxidation is uncertain and may require additional fine-tuning in experimental trials.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat samples on identical substrates: one using standard HVOF parameters (control) and one using the optimized parameters (reduced stand-off distance, increased particle velocity/temperature). Ensure all other conditions (feedstock size, substrate preparation, ambient atmosphere) are held constant. After deposition, measure the coating thickness, microstructure (using SEM and cross-sectional analysis), and oxidation levels (using XPS or EDS) for both groups.
measurements: Porosity and adhesion quality via SEM
Oxide scale composition and extent via XPS/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized HVOF parameters do not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness beyond the baseline 15–45 μm range, or if the as-sprayed oxidation levels are significantly higher (i.e., they compromise coating integrity or exceed predetermined oxidation thresholds), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

reading.lever: Optimize HVOF spraying parameters (stand-off distance, particle velocity/temperature) to boost deposited thickness while limiting oxidation.
reading.why: HVOF optimization has produced thicker, denser HEA coatings with minimal oxidation in related systems, addressing the thickness shortfall without compromising integrity.
